title: The Chaldeans
hookLine: Iraq's Catholics still pray in a form of Aramaic; Francis visited them in 2021

cards: "Talitha cumi." Jesus takes a dead girl by the hand and says those words, and she gets up. Mark's Gospel sets them down as they sounded, then translates: damsel, arise.
He leaves the words standing, like stones in a field, so a reader hears the voice. Readers take them as Aramaic, the speech of Jesus's world.
Now go to a village church on the plain near Mosul, in northern Iraq, or a church in Baghdad.
On Sunday, priest and people pray in Syriac, a form of Aramaic: words from the same family as talitha cumi, still in the mouths of a living congregation.

teach.b: The name reaches back to Abraham. Genesis says his family set out from Ur of the Chaldeans, and the Chaldean Catholic Church takes its name from that old region, in what is now Iraq.
Its people speak of themselves as heirs of some of the earliest Christian communities of Mesopotamia. Then the language. Mark keeps Aramaic more than once.
On the cross, he writes, Jesus cried, "Eloi, Eloi, lamma sabacthani?" and then translates it: my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?

Syriac, the language of the Chaldean liturgy, is a form of Aramaic, written in its own script. When Chaldeans pray the Our Father in Syriac, the sound is a near neighbor of the sound in that Galilean house.
Then the hard years. Iraq's Christians have lived through war, and in recent years families fled when an extremist group overran their towns on the Nineveh Plain. Churches were burned.
Some families came back to rebuild; others now pray in Syriac far from home. And then a visit.
Pope Francis traveled to Iraq, prayed among the ruins of Mosul's churches, and went to Ur, the place of Abraham, to pray with Muslims, Yazidis and others who honor Abraham too.

Look back at this week: a Divine Liturgy sung almost entirely, a wall of icons, a baby given everything at once, a priest's wife with a title, cedars in Lebanon, Thomas's children in India, and now Chaldeans in Iraq.
One Catholic Church, many ancient homes.

how: Chaldean Catholics celebrate the Holy Qurbana in the East Syriac tradition, praying in Syriac and Arabic and, abroad, in local languages; their patriarch is based in Baghdad, and Chaldean parishes abroad serve families who left Iraq.

games.q: you're a pope visiting Iraq, among churches still scarred by war. where do you go to pray with people of other faiths?
o: only a cathedral in the capital.
nowhere: you pray only with Catholics.
games.why: Pope Francis went to Ur, where Genesis says Abraham's family set out, and prayed there with Muslims, Yazidis and others who honor Abraham.

practice: Picture a church with smoke stains on its walls and a family sweeping the floor anyway, then the rivers, the markets, and the neighbors of every faith who've also lost homes.

If you pray, pray for Iraq and everyone who lives there, or say the Our Father slowly, knowing it's prayed in Syriac somewhere today. If you don't, sit with the people sweeping that floor, and wish them a whole roof.

wordCard.voice: The Chaldeans. Iraq's Eastern Catholic church, named for the land of Abraham, praying in Syriac, a form of Aramaic. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic words written in Greek letters in Mark 5:41, which the Douay-Rheims translates: damsel, arise.

carryVoice: Your line: the language of jesus. Talitha cumi, the words Mark left standing. Until tomorrow.
